rv.q: If you have any interest in the power of theatre, I urge you to catch a play that’s both an exploration of it and a remarkable vindication of it.
Jack Thorne's 'The Motive and the Cue,' is a rapier-witted and stirring love-letter to theatre, and to Hamlet, and to two of the play'
That ‘The Motive and The Cue’ has fast become almost as acclaimed seems so very fitting.

Flynn, in roll-neck sweaters, occasionally just his underpants, has Burton’s voice and volatility off to a tee. Middleton is a dazzling, kooky Elizabeth Taylor, a performance that has improved on this transfer. But it is Gatiss’s marvellous Gielgud - posh, prickly and buttoned-up - who makes the evening vibrate.
It is the triumph of both play and performance that he is so much more than that.
The clash of these two theatrical greats, along with the glimpse behind the curtain of the creative process makes The Motive and the Cue a perfect production for any lover of theatre to experience.
One thing is for sure: it’s a play that epitomises the epithet ‘A love letter to theatre’.
Bolstered by immaculate work from its leads and a sharp, insightful script, it will likely be a late entry to many end of the year lists.
Lifting the curtain on the rehearsal room and witnessing the process, rather than watching the end product, makes this an absolute must see for all theatre lovers.
The resulting shape of The Motive and the Cue is both polished and full-blooded.
Gatiss’ Gielgud, lonely and closeted, feels like a has-been while at home Burton drowns himself in alcohol with his new bride Elizabeth Taylor, played sultrily by Tuppence Middleton.

cn.t: Jack Thorne's meta-theatrical drama about Burton and Gielgud's 1964 Hamlet rehearsals wins acclaim for its sharp script and immaculate performances, particularly from its leads, in this insightful peek behind the curtain of theatrical history.
